holidays.name: National Yorkshire Pudding Day
holidays.description: This is a salute to the golden, puffed-up British classic that rises dramatically in a hot oven. It's a crispy-edged cup with a soft middle, made for holding gravy. Bakers cheer when it climbs, and cry a little when it flops.
holidays.origin: Yorkshire pudding first showed up in English cookbooks in the 1700s. It began as a thrifty way to stretch a meal by catching the drippings from roasting meat. The day itself is an unofficial food observance.
holidays.funFact: Despite the name, it isn't a dessert. It's traditionally served with roast beef, and the batter is just eggs, flour, and milk or water.

holidays.name: International Skeptics Day
holidays.description: This is a day to raise an eyebrow at everything, in the best way. It encourages people to ask for evidence, question big claims, and think critically before believing the internet, a rumor, or your uncle's miracle cure.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial observance, often credited to eventologist Adrienne Sioux Koopersmith, who invented thousands of quirky special days. Its roots are in the long tradition of skeptical inquiry.
holidays.funFact: The word skeptic comes from the Greek skeptikos, meaning inquiring or thoughtful. Ancient skeptics were basically history's first professional question-askers.

holidays.name: National M&M Day
holidays.description: This day celebrates the candy-coated chocolate bits that melt in your mouth and not in your hand. Fans mark it with handfuls of them, trail mix, cookies, and the ongoing debate over which color tastes best.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial food observance of unclear origin. It honors the candy that debuted in 1941.
holidays.funFact: The name comes from the last names of Forrest Mars and Bruce Murrie, the two men behind the candy.
